603.title: Kaddish is praise
603.hook: an Aramaic prayer praising God, said by mourners, that never mentions death
603.howItsDone: Kaddish is said only with a minyan: the leader or the mourners recite it, and the congregation answers amen and the line y'hei shmeh rabba aloud. Different forms of it mark the sections of the service, close the Amidah, follow study, and are said by mourners.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aleinu, the prayer that bows near the end of the service. Your line was our duty to praise. What did you praise out loud? Today, a prayer people think they know. Day six hundred three.

Ask most people what the Kaddish is and they'll say: the Jewish prayer for the dead. It's in films, in novels, in the scene at the graveside. And it's true that mourners say it. But read the words, and something strange happens. There is no death in it. No grave, no loss, no person who has died, no afterlife. It doesn't ask for comfort. It doesn't even mention the mourner. From beginning to end, it does one thing. It praises God.
screen: `THE PRAYER FOR THE DEAD?` → `NO DEATH IN IT.` → `ONLY PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Kaddish means holy, or sanctification. It's in Aramaic, the everyday language many Jews spoke in the time of the Talmud, not Hebrew. Its first words are yitgadal v'yitkadash shmeh rabba: magnified and sanctified be his great name. Those two verbs echo a line in Ezekiel, in the old Jewish translation: "Thus will I magnify Myself, and sanctify Myself." Then the prayer asks that God's kingship be established in our lives and our days, soon. And at the center comes the line the whole congregation answers aloud: y'hei shmeh rabba, may his great name be blessed forever and ever. The Talmud treats that answer as huge. In tractate Shabbat, a teacher says that whoever answers it with all their strength has a harsh decree against them torn up. Kaddish likely began not in mourning but in the study house: after a teacher finished a lesson, everyone praised God together. That version is still said today, after learning. In the service it appears in several forms. A short one marks the joints between sections, like a bookmark. A full one closes the main prayer. One is said after study. And one is said by mourners. So when a mourner stands up, they aren't saying a prayer about death. They are leading the room in praise, at the very moment praise is hardest. Tomorrow, why they do it.
screen: `KADDISH: HOLY, IN ARAMAIC.` · `MAGNIFIED AND SANCTIFIED.` · `THE ROOM ANSWERS: MAY HIS NAME BE BLESSED.` · `FROM THE STUDY HOUSE.` · then, large: `NO DEATH IN IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer amen to a praise. Settle, and breathe. Bring back someone's words of praise you heard recently. A friend saying the sunset was beautiful. A child proud of a drawing. A grandparent thanking God for a meal. Hear it again in your mind. Then answer it, quietly: amen. Yes. So be it. In the Kaddish, the answering is half the prayer. Let yourself be the one who answers. The bell holds the time.
Kaddish. Holy, sanctification. An Aramaic prayer of pure praise, said by mourners and answered by everyone.
Your line: magnified and sanctified. Today, when someone praises anything good, a meal, a song, a day, answer it with a real yes. Day six hundred three.

604.title: Why mourners say it
604.hook: after a parent dies, many say Kaddish for eleven months and each year after, with a minyan answering
604.howItsDone: Mourners say the Mourner's Kaddish at daily services with a minyan, traditionally for eleven months after a parent's death and on each yahrzeit; many congregations make sure a minyan gathers so mourners can say it, and the congregation answers aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kaddish: an Aramaic prayer of praise with no death in it. Your line was magnified and sanctified. Did you answer someone's praise with a yes? Today, why mourners say it anyway. Day six hundred four.

It's a Tuesday morning, seven a.m., in a small synagogue. Nine people are waiting, checking the door. A woman whose father died last month needs ten to say Kaddish. Someone makes a phone call. A neighbor comes in, still in running clothes, and sits down. Now there are ten. She stands, and says the words. And as she pauses, the room answers her, out loud. This happens in towns all over the world, every morning and every evening, for months on end. Why does a mourner need a room full of people to say one prayer?
screen: `NINE PEOPLE WAITING.` → `A NEIGHBOR IN RUNNING CLOTHES.` → `NOW THERE ARE TEN.`

segments.voice: Start with the rule. Kaddish is a prayer of holiness, and Jewish law says those are said only with a minyan, a quorum of ten. So a mourner can't say it alone. That's not a technicality. It means the mourner has to come out of the house, and the community has to show up. How did the Kaddish become the mourner's prayer at all? A medieval story is told about Rabbi Akiva. He meets a dead man's soul carrying wood, in torment. Akiva finds the man's young son, teaches him to stand in the congregation and lead the praise, and the father's soul is released. The story spread through medieval Europe, and the custom spread with it. How long? Many say Kaddish for eleven months after a parent dies. Tradition held that judgment of a soul could last up to twelve months, and children stop at eleven so as not to suggest their parent needed the full year. Then, every year on the anniversary of the death, the yahrzeit, they say it again. Who says it? In many communities, sons and daughters both; in Orthodox communities, customs for daughters differ from place to place. And what does it do for the mourner? Look at the words. At the hardest moment of their life, a mourner stands and says: may God's name be magnified. They don't have to feel it. They just have to say it, and the room answers. The answering holds them up.
screen: `ONLY WITH TEN.` · `A STORY ABOUT RABBI AKIVA.` · `ELEVEN MONTHS, THEN EACH YAHRZEIT.` · `THE ROOM HOLDS THEM UP.` · then, large: `THE COMMUNITY ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of someone who says Kaddish. Settle, and breathe. Maybe it's a friend who lost a parent this year. Maybe it's you, or someone in your family who stood up years ago. Picture them standing in a room, saying words of praise while they grieve. Now picture yourself in that room, as one of the ten. Hold them in mind for the rest of the sit. If you can, send them a message today. The bell holds the time.
Why mourners say it. Because praise said in grief needs ten people to answer it, and the answering carries the mourner.
Your line: the community answers. Today, be one of the ten for someone: a call, a visit, a meal, or just showing up. Day six hundred four.

605.title: Adon Olam
605.hook: a medieval poem ending in trust: the Lord is with me, I shall not fear
605.howItsDone: Adon Olam opens the morning service in many prayer books and is often sung at the end of Shabbat and festival services, to many different melodies; it also appears in the bedtime Shema in many traditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why mourners say the Kaddish, and why it takes ten. Your line was the community answers. Did you show up for someone? Today, a song that starts with the universe and ends at your pillow. Day six hundred five.

Here's a party trick from Jewish summer camps. Pick almost any tune. A folk song, a pop chorus, a sea shanty. And somebody will fit Adon Olam to it. The poem's lines are so even, so regular, that the words slide onto nearly any melody. So in many synagogues it's sung to a different tune every week, often at the very end of the Shabbat service, kids running up front to sing it. It's light, it's bouncy. And it's about some of the biggest ideas in the prayer book.
screen: `ANY TUNE WILL DO.` → `KIDS RUN UP TO SING IT.` → `THE BIGGEST IDEAS.`

segments.voice: Adon olam means Lord of the world, or Master of the universe. Nobody knows for sure who wrote it. It's sometimes credited to Solomon ibn Gabirol, a great poet of eleventh-century Spain, but the evidence is thin. It's medieval, and its even meter is the kind Hebrew poets in Spain used. The poem moves like a camera zooming in. It begins before anything existed: Lord of the world, who reigned before any form was made. Then, without beginning, without end. God, vast and alone. And then, halfway through, the voice turns. He is my God, my living redeemer, the rock in my time of trouble. Suddenly it isn't the universe. It's me. And the last lines come down to the smallest scene there is. Into his hand I entrust my spirit, when I sleep and when I wake. And with my spirit, my body too. The Lord is with me; I shall not fear. Those last lines lean on two psalms. In the old Jewish translation, Psalm 31: "Into Thy hand I commit my spirit." And Psalm 118: "The LORD is for me; I will not fear." That's why Adon Olam is also part of the bedtime prayers in many prayer books. You hand over your spirit for the night, and expect it back in the morning. A poem about infinity, ending with someone falling asleep without fear.
screen: `LORD OF THE WORLD.` · `BEFORE ANY FORM WAS MADE.` · `THE VOICE TURNS: MY GOD.` · `INTO HIS HAND, WHEN I SLEEP.` · then, large: `I SHALL NOT FEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing one closing song. Pick any tune you know well, one that's easy in your mouth. If you know Adon Olam, sing its last line to it, quietly. If not, just hum the tune and hold the meaning: I shall not fear. Sing it twice. Then let the song fade, and sit in the quiet after it, the way a room does when the service ends. The bell holds the time.
Adon Olam. Lord of the world. A medieval poem that zooms from eternity to one person falling asleep in trust.
Your line: I shall not fear. Tonight, as you lie down, say it once before you sleep. Day six hundred five.

606.title: Yigdal
606.hook: Maimonides' thirteen principles put into verse
606.howItsDone: Yigdal is printed at the start of the morning service in many prayer books and is often sung at the end of Friday night and festival evening services; a prose version of the thirteen principles, each beginning 'I believe with perfect faith', appears in many siddurim.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Adon Olam, the poem that ends with sleep. Your line was I shall not fear. Did you say it at bedtime? Today, its partner, a song that holds a whole philosophy. Day six hundred six.

Picture a philosophy textbook. Dense, careful, footnoted, written in Arabic by a doctor in twelfth-century Egypt. Now picture a congregation on a Friday night, swaying, singing it to a bright melody. That's what happened to Maimonides' thirteen principles of faith. A list he wrote as a commentary on the Mishnah, arguing about what a Jew must hold to be true, became, about a century and a half later, a short Hebrew song. In many synagogues it's sung at the end of Friday night services. Philosophy, set to music.
screen: `A DOCTOR'S ARGUMENT IN EGYPT.` → `THIRTEEN PRINCIPLES.` → `SET TO MUSIC.`

segments.voice: Yigdal means may he be magnified. It opens: magnified be the living God, and praised. The poem is usually credited to Daniel ben Judah, who lived in Rome in the fourteenth century. He did something clever. He took Maimonides' thirteen principles and gave each one a line. God exists. God is one. God has no body. God is first and last. Only God is to be worshipped. The prophets spoke truly. Moses was the greatest of the prophets. The Torah was given from heaven. It won't be exchanged. God knows our deeds. God rewards and punishes. The redeemer will come. And the dead will live again. Thirteen beliefs, thirteen lines, and the last line ends the song with the hope of life after death. Now the honest part. Maimonides' list was never the only way to say what Judaism believes. In the centuries after him, other great thinkers argued with it. Joseph Albo, in fifteenth-century Spain, boiled the roots of faith down to three. Others asked whether faith can be a checklist at all, when so much of Judaism is about what you do. Still, the list stuck, partly because of songs like this one, and a prose version beginning I believe with perfect faith is printed in many prayer books after the morning service. Yigdal turns a debate into something a child can sing. That's how ideas travel in this tradition: not only in books, but in the mouth.
screen: `MAY HE BE MAGNIFIED.` · `THIRTEEN PRINCIPLES, THIRTEEN LINES.` · `OTHERS ARGUED: ALBO SAID THREE.` · `A DEBATE A CHILD CAN SING.` · then, large: `FAITH IN VERSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say one thing you believe aloud. Settle, and breathe. Don't reach for the biggest belief you have. Reach for one that's true for you today. It might be about God, or about people, or about how you want to live. It might be a doubt that you hold honestly. Put it into one short sentence. Then say it out loud, once, quietly. Hear what it sounds like in the air instead of in your head. Then let it rest. The bell holds the time.
Yigdal. May he be magnified. Maimonides' thirteen principles of faith, set as a thirteen-line song.
Your line: faith in verse. Today, notice one belief you carry because of a song, a rhyme or a saying, not a book. Day six hundred six.

607.title: None like our God
607.hook: a simple song with a repeating tune
607.howItsDone: Ein Keloheinu is sung near the end of the Shabbat and festival morning service in most Ashkenazi synagogues, and said daily in many Sephardi communities; it is usually followed by a Talmud passage about the Temple incense.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yigdal, thirteen principles in thirteen lines. Your line was faith in verse. What belief did you notice that came to you in a song? Today, the simplest song in the service. Day six hundred seven.

Some songs are built to be learned in one hearing. A lullaby. A chant at a ball game. Ein Keloheinu is one of those. A child who can't read Hebrew yet can sing it by the second verse. The same handful of words come around again and again, with only the first word changing. And the tune most Ashkenazi synagogues use rolls along like a march. It's often sung near the very end of Shabbat morning services. But the simple song hides a puzzle, and a tiny secret.
screen: `LEARNED IN ONE HEARING.` → `ONLY THE FIRST WORD CHANGES.` → `A PUZZLE AND A SECRET.`

segments.voice: Ein keloheinu means there is none like our God. The song goes: none like our God, none like our Lord, none like our King, none like our Savior. Then the next verse swaps the first word: who is like our God? Who is like our Lord? Then: let us give thanks to our God. Then: blessed is our God. And last: you are our God. Five verses, four names each time. Here's the puzzle. Why say there is none like our God first, and only then ask who is like our God? Shouldn't the question come before the answer? Commentators explain the order on purpose: you state it first, so that when you ask, the question is wonder, not doubt. You already know the answer. You're just enjoying asking. Now the secret. Look at the first letters of the first three verses in Hebrew: ein, mi, nodeh. Aleph, mem, nun. Together they spell amen. Hidden in the song is the word people say to agree with a blessing. There's one more explanation people give. On weekdays the main prayer has nineteen blessings, but on Shabbat only seven. Some say this song, with its many names of God, helps make up the hundred blessings the Talmud asks for each day. Customs differ: Ashkenazim usually sing it on Shabbat and festivals, and many Sephardim say it every day. Either way, it's a song you can't sing wrong.
screen: `NONE LIKE OUR GOD.` · `FIRST THE ANSWER, THEN THE QUESTION.` · `EIN, MI, NODEH SPELL AMEN.` · `HELPING MAKE A HUNDRED BLESSINGS.` · then, large: `NONE LIKE HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing a line over and over. Settle, and breathe. Choose one short line. If you know it, ein keloheinu. If not, the English: none like our God. Or any short line that means something to you. Say or sing it slowly, then again, then again. Don't add anything. Let the repetition do the work. After a while, notice whether the words get lighter, or heavier, or simply quieter. Then stop, and sit with the echo. The bell holds the time.
Ein keloheinu. There is none like our God. A five-verse song that hides the word amen in its first letters.
Your line: none like him. Today, when something truly one of a kind catches you, a face, a sky, a voice, say none like it. Day six hundred seven.

608.title: The afternoon pause (Berakhot 6b)
608.hook: a few minutes in the working day; the Talmud says to be especially careful with this prayer
608.carry: pray in the middle of the day
608.howItsDone: Mincha is said daily from early afternoon until sunset: Ashrei (Psalm 145), the silent Amidah with its repetition when there is a minyan, and on most weekdays Tachanun and Aleinu. Many people gather for it at work or between errands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ein Keloheinu, the song that hides amen in its first letters. Your line was none like him. What one-of-a-kind thing did you notice? Today we leave the morning behind. Day six hundred eight.

Three-fifteen on a weekday. The inbox is full. A meeting just ran long, the kids need picking up, the coffee's gone cold. Nobody plans anything holy for three-fifteen. Morning has its own mood, fresh and new. Night has its own mood, quiet and closing. But the middle of the afternoon is pure busyness. And that's exactly where Jewish tradition puts one of its three daily prayers. In office buildings in some cities, you can find a small group gathering in a conference room for ten minutes, then going back to their desks.
screen: `THREE-FIFTEEN ON A WEEKDAY.` → `NOBODY PLANS ANYTHING HOLY.` → `TEN MINUTES IN A CONFERENCE ROOM.`

segments.voice: The afternoon prayer is called Mincha. The word means a gift, or an offering. In the Temple, a meal offering was brought in the afternoon, and the prayer took its name from that time of day. It's short: a psalm, the Amidah said silently, and on most weekdays a few closing lines. Ten or fifteen minutes. The Talmud links each daily prayer to one of the ancestors, and gives the afternoon to Isaac. In Genesis, in the old Jewish translation, "Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." The rabbis read that meditation as prayer. Isaac, alone in a field toward evening, before he even sees Rebekah coming. Now the line from the Talmud this day is named for. In tractate Berakhot, page 6b, a teacher says in the name of another: a person should always be especially careful with the afternoon prayer. Why this one? Later commentators give a plain answer. Morning prayer comes before the day starts, and evening prayer comes after it ends. But Mincha lands right in the middle, when you're busiest and it's easiest to let it slip. Being careful with it means stepping out of the stream on purpose. The Talmud gives its own reason too, a story about a prophet on a mountain, and that's tomorrow. Today, just the shape of it: a gift given in the middle of the day.
screen: `MINCHA: A GIFT, AN OFFERING.` · `ISAAC IN THE FIELD AT EVENTIDE.` · `BE ESPECIALLY CAREFUL WITH IT.` · `THE BUSIEST HOUR.` · then, large: `PRAY IN THE MIDDLE OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pause mid-afternoon. If it's afternoon now, good. If not, practice it here, and set a reminder for later. Stop what you're doing. Stand or sit up straight. Close your eyes. Breathe out the last hour. If you pray, this is a moment for it, in any words you have. If you don't, just stand in the middle of your day like Isaac in his field, and look around. The bell holds the time.
Mincha. A gift, an offering. The short afternoon prayer, said in the busiest part of the day.
Your line: pray in the middle of the day. Set one alarm for mid-afternoon today, and when it rings, stop for one full minute. Day six hundred eight.

609.title: Elijah was answered (1 Kings 18:36)
609.hook: Elijah's prayer on Mount Carmel came at the time of the afternoon offering
609.howItsDone: Many Jews take the Talmud's teaching about Mincha seriously by gathering for it at work or setting a fixed time; at the close of Yom Kippur the congregation calls out 'the LORD, He is God' seven times, the people's words from Mount Carmel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mincha, the gift in the middle of the day. Your line was pray in the middle of the day. Did your afternoon alarm ring? Today, the story the Talmud gives for why. Day six hundred nine.
screen: `PRAY IN THE MIDDLE OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: A mountain on the coast, three years into a drought. The ground is cracked. Crowds have climbed Mount Carmel to watch a contest. On one side, hundreds of prophets of the god Baal. On the other, one man: Elijah. Two altars, two bulls, and no fire on either. Whoever's god answers with fire, that god is God. All morning the other side calls out. Noon comes. Nothing. Elijah waits. He waits all the way into the afternoon.
screen: `THREE YEARS OF DROUGHT.` → `TWO ALTARS, NO FIRE.` → `ELIJAH WAITS.`

segments.voice: When it's finally his turn, Elijah does something strange. He rebuilds an old broken altar with twelve stones, one for each tribe. He digs a trench. Then he has the offering drenched with water, three times, until the trench overflows. In a drought, he pours out water. No one can say the fire was a trick. Then the verse that gives this day its name. In the old Jewish translation: "And it came to pass at the time of the offering of the evening offering, that Elijah the prophet came near." That's the afternoon offering, the same hour as Mincha. And his prayer is short. "Hear me, O LORD, hear me." In Hebrew, aneni, answer me, said twice. Fire falls, and burns up the offering, the stones, the dust, and licks up the water in the trench. The people fall on their faces and cry out: "The LORD, He is God; the LORD, He is God." Now back to yesterday's line from the Talmud. Berakhot 6b says to be especially careful with the afternoon prayer, and gives this as the reason: Elijah was answered only at Mincha. The prayer that's easiest to skip is the one the Bible shows being answered. One more echo. At the very end of Yom Kippur, after a whole day of prayer, congregations call out the words the people cried on Carmel, the LORD, He is God, seven times. A mountaintop cry, said in late afternoon light, still.
screen: `TWELVE STONES, AND WATER.` · `AT THE AFTERNOON OFFERING.` · `ANSWER ME, ANSWER ME.` · `THE LORD, HE IS GOD.` · then, large: `HEARD IN THE AFTERNOON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask in as few words as you can. Settle, and breathe. Elijah's prayer was two short verses. Not a speech. Think of one thing you would ask for, if you could ask, in the fewest words possible. Say it inside, or aloud. If you pray, you can use Elijah's own words: hear me, O LORD, hear me. Then stop asking and simply wait, the way he waited, in the quiet after. The bell holds the time.
Elijah was answered. On Mount Carmel, at the hour of the afternoon offering, which is why the Talmud says to treasure Mincha.
Your line: heard in the afternoon. A week of Kaddish, mourners, Adon Olam, Yigdal, Ein Keloheinu, Mincha and Elijah. This afternoon, keep your pause, and keep it short. Day six hundred nine.

it was short: hear me, O LORD, hear me.
Elijah had his offering soaked with water
three times, until the trench overflowed.
Yom Kippur ends with the people's cry from Carmel
the LORD, He is God, said seven times.

fork.setup: you're Elijah. it's a drought, and you need fire to fall on your altar. what do you do first?
options: soak the offering with water, three times.
fork.reveal: he drenched it until the trench overflowed, then prayed briefly at the time of the afternoon offering.

original.note: Hebrew: answer me. Elijah says it twice on Mount Carmel.

trapdoor: what you thought: an action story about fire from heaven.
what it means: a short prayer, said at the afternoon offering, that was answered.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 6b reads 1 Kings 18:36 as the reason to treasure Mincha; Neilah ends with 18:39 repeated seven times.
